logs: Windows Security Event 4624 (successful logon) — Logon Type 3 Authentication Package NTLM
Windows Security Event 4625 (failed logon) — brute force / scanning attempts
Windows Security Event 4776 (NTLM authentication attempt) — domain controller NTLM auth
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) — SMB (port 445) WMI (port 135) WinRM (port 5985)
Windows Event 8004 (NTLM authentication) for NTLM audit logging
detection_rules: Sigma: win_pass_the_hash_ntlm — Event 4624 Logon Type 3 with NTLM auth from unexpected host
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=4624 LogonType=3 AuthenticationPackage=NTLM | stats by Computer TargetUserName IpAddress
Sigma: win_ntlm_relay — Event 4624 where source and destination are unexpected for the account
Baseline: alert on NTLM auth from systems that normally use Kerberos
controls: Enable SMB Signing on all systems

topics.gap_analysis: NTLM is still widely used in many environments — disabling it entirely breaks applications. PtH is silent because it uses legitimate NTLM authentication. Gap: many orgs dont monitor NTLM usage patterns to distinguish PtH from legitimate auth. NTLM relay can be defeated with SMB Signing but many orgs havent enforced it globally.
drills: Execute PtH using netexec with a stolen hash. Examine Event 4624 — verify Logon Type 3 with NTLM authentication. Write a Sigma rule to detect NTLM logons from unexpected sources. Then enable SMB Signing and attempt NTLM relay — verify it fails.
common_mistakes: Not distinguishing NTLM from Kerberos in Event 4624 — they look similar without checking Authentication Package field
Only looking at failed logons (4625) and missing successful PtH (4624)
Not enforcing SMB Signing globally (partial deployment doesnt help)

topics.title: RDP Lateral Movement (T1021.001) vs. RDP Session Monitoring
concepts: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP): graphical remote access commonly used for lateral movement
Attackers use RDP for interactive lateral movement especially after obtaining credentials
RDP hijacking: stealing active RDP sessions via tscon (T1563.002)
Detection: monitor RDP connections (Event 4624 Logon Type 10) source/destination and session activity
RDP over reverse proxy and RDP through SSH tunnels are also used
key_facts: Event 4624 Logon Type 10 (RemoteInteractive) indicates RDP logon
Event 4778 (session reconnection) and 4779 (session disconnect) track RDP session state
tscon session_id /dest:other_session allows stealing RDP sessions without password (requires SYSTEM)
TerminalServices-* event logs provide detailed RDP session information

attack_side.technique: Use RDP for lateral movement to interactively control target systems
attack_steps: Obtain valid credentials (via credential theft brute force or phishing)
Connect via RDP: mstsc /v:target_ip or xfreerdp /v:target /u:user
RDP session hijacking: query user (find sessions) then tscon session /dest:SESSIONNAME
Use RDP for data exfiltration via clipboard drive mapping or file transfer
Pivot through RDP to additional systems

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect RDP connections from unexpected sources session hijacking via tscon and brute-force RDP attempts
logs: Windows Security Event 4624 (Logon Type 10 = RemoteInteractive) — RDP logon
Windows Security Event 4625 (failed logon Type 10) — RDP brute force
Windows TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational Event 21 22 25 (RDP session events)
Sysmon Event 1 (tscon.exe execution — session hijacking indicator)
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) — port 3389 connections
detection_rules: Sigma: win_rdp_logon_from_unexpected_source — Event 4624 Logon Type 10 from unexpected IP
Sigma: win_tscon_session_hijack — tscon.exe execution indicating RDP session hijacking
Sigma: win_rdp_brute_force — Event 4625 Logon Type 10 count > threshold in time window
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=4624 LogonType=10 | stats by IpAddress TargetUserName Computer
controls: Restrict RDP via firewall (only from jump boxes)

topics.gap_analysis: RDP session hijacking (tscon) is hard to detect because the session appears to continue normally. BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) allowed unauthenticated RDP code execution. Gap: many orgs dont enforce NLA allowing pre-authentication attacks. RDP over non-standard ports (port redirection) evades simple port-based monitoring.
drills: Connect via RDP to a target with stolen credentials. Verify Event 4624 Logon Type 10 fires. Then perform tscon session hijacking — verify Sysmon Event 1 captures tscon.exe. Write Sigma rules for both. Implement RDP Gateway and show how it adds MFA.
common_mistakes: Not distinguishing Logon Type 10 (RDP) from Type 7 (credential delegation) in Event 4624
Allowing RDP from any source (no jump box / ZTNA)
Not enforcing NLA which prevents many RDP-based attacks

topics.title: Pass-the-Ticket (T1550.003) vs. Kerberos Event Monitoring
concepts: Pass-the-Ticket (PtT): inject a stolen Kerberos ticket into the current logon session to authenticate as another user
Tickets can be Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) for domain-wide access or Service Ticket (TGS) for specific services
Golden Ticket: forged TGT using the krbtgt hash — grants persistent domain admin access
Silver Ticket: forged TGS using a service account hash — grants access to specific services
Detection: monitor for tickets with anomalies (wrong encryption impossible session forged PAC)
key_facts: Kerberos tickets are stored in the LSASS process memory and can be injected via Mimikatz kerberos::ptt
Golden Ticket TGTs can be forged for any user including non-existent ones — valid as long as krbtgt hash is known
Event 4769 (TGS Request) and 4768 (TGT Request) log Kerberos activity
Event 4624 Logon Type 3 with Kerberos authentication may indicate PtT

attack_side.technique: Inject stolen or forged Kerberos tickets to authenticate as another user without their password
attack_steps: Obtain tickets: extract from LSASS (Mimikatz sekurlsa::tickets) or forge them
Golden Ticket: Mimikatz kerberos::golden /user:Administrator /domain:corp /sid:S-1-5... /krbtgt:hash /ptt
Silver Ticket: forge TGS for specific service using service account hash
Inject ticket: Mimikatz kerberos::ptt ticket.kirbi or Rubeus ptt /ticket:base64
Access services as the ticketed user — no password or hash needed for authentication

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect forged/stolen ticket usage: tickets from unexpected systems ticket anomalies and impossible session patterns
logs: Windows Security Event 4768 (Kerberos TGT Request) — ticket request from unexpected host
Windows Security Event 4769 (Kerberos TGS Request) — service ticket request with anomalies
Windows Security Event 4624 (Logon Type 3 with Kerberos) — network logon using Kerberos
Sysmon Event 1 (Mimikatz or Rubeus execution for ticket injection)
detection_rules: Sigma: win_kerberos_golden_ticket — Event 4769 for a user account not in AD (forged ticket)
Sigma: win_pass_the_hash_kerberos — Event 4624 Kerberos logon from unexpected source
Splunk: index=windows EventCode=4768 OR EventCode=4769 | where match(IpAddress unexpected)
Detect ticket lifetime anomalies: tickets with 10-year expiry (common in forged tickets)
tools: Microsoft Defender for Identity (Golden/Silver Ticket detection)
controls: Regular krbtgt password resets (twice to invalidate old tickets)

topics.gap_analysis: Forged tickets (Golden/Silver) are very hard to detect because they are cryptographically valid. Detection focuses on behavioral anomalies: tickets used from unexpected locations tickets for disabled/deleted accounts or tickets with unusual lifetimes. Gap: krbtgt must be reset TWICE (not once) to invalidate existing Golden Tickets. Many orgs dont know this.
drills: Forge a Golden Ticket using Mimikatz with the krbtgt hash (from DCSync lab). Inject and use it to access a DC. Examine Event 4769 — what anomalies are visible? Write a detection for tickets with abnormally long lifetimes. Then reset krbtgt twice and show the Golden Ticket is invalidated.
common_mistakes: Not resetting krbtgt twice (once leaves the old hash active)
Only monitoring TGS (4769) and not TGT (4768) events
Not investigating tickets for accounts that dont exist in AD (clear sign of forgery)

modules.title: Collection & Exfiltration — Data Staging & Theft vs. FIM, DLP & Egress Monitoring
modules.objective: Learner can execute data collection and exfiltration techniques and build detections using file integrity monitoring, DLP, and network egress analysis.

topics.title: Data Staging (T1074) vs. File Integrity Monitoring
concepts: Data staging: collecting data from multiple locations into a single directory before exfiltration
Attackers use temp directories recycle bin or hidden folders for staging
Common staging: copy sensitive files to C:\Users\Public\ or %TEMP% then archive (zip rar 7z)
File Integrity Monitoring (FIM): monitors file system changes — creation modification deletion
Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) and Event 2 (FileCreationTimeChanged) detect staging activity
key_facts: Attackers prefer staging in directories with high noise (temp public) to blend in
Compressing staged data reduces exfiltration time and evades size-based DLP
Sysmon Event 11 can monitor specific directories for file creation
Data staging often involves unusual file access patterns — bulk reads of sensitive directories

attack_side.technique: Collect and stage sensitive data from across the network into a central location for exfiltration
attack_steps: Discover sensitive data: search file shares databases email browser profiles
Copy data to staging directory: copy *.docx C:\Users\Public\Staging\
Archive data: 7z a -p archive.7z C:\Users\Public\Staging\* (password-protected)
Stage on a single system for exfiltration (T1074.002 Remote Data Staging)
Delete original copies to cover tracks (optional)

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect bulk file copy operations archive creation in unusual locations and unusual file access patterns
logs: Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) — files created in staging directories (temp public recycle bin)
Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) — archive tools (7z.exe winrar.exe) executing with unusual arguments
Windows Security Event 4663 (Object Access) — file access auditing on sensitive directories
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) — data transfer to staging system
detection_rules: Sigma: file_create_win_data_staging — Event 11 with many files created in temp/public directories in short time
Sigma: proc_creation_win_archive_tool_in_temp — 7z.exe or rar.exe executing from temp directories
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename=*C:\Users\Public\* | stats count by Computer | where count > 50
FIM: alert on bulk file modifications in sensitive directories
controls: File access auditing on sensitive directories

topics.gap_analysis: Data staging in noisy directories (temp public) blends with normal activity. Archive creation is common for legitimate purposes. Gap: FIM tools monitor for changes but may not detect bulk READ access to sensitive data. Must correlate file access with subsequent staging and archive creation.
drills: Stage 50 files from a file share to C:\Users\Public\Staging\. Archive with 7z. Check which Sysmon events fire. Write Sigma rules for bulk file creation in staging areas and archive tool execution from non-standard paths.
common_mistakes: Only monitoring file creation not file READ access to sensitive data
Not alerting on archive tool usage in unusual contexts
Missing remote data staging (data collected on one system staged on another)

topics.title: Exfiltration Over C2 (T1041) & Web Services (T1567) vs. DLP & Egress Filtering
concepts: Exfiltration over C2 channel: encoding data into the existing C2 communication (HTTPS beacons DNS queries)
Exfiltration over web services: uploading data to legitimate cloud storage (Mega Dropbox Google Drive S3)
DLP (Data Loss Prevention): monitors egress traffic and endpoints for sensitive data patterns
Egress filtering: restrict outbound connections to known/allowed destinations
Network-based detection: monitor for unusual outbound data volume beaconing patterns and new destinations
key_facts: Median time from initial access to exfiltration is under 2 days (2024 incident data)
Data encoded in DNS queries (DNS tunneling) bypasses HTTPS-based DLP
Cloud exfiltration to legitimate services (Mega AWS S3) may not be on blocklists
Zeek http.log and ssl.log capture outbound web traffic metadata for analysis

attack_side.technique: Exfiltrate staged data over the C2 channel or via web services encoding to evade detection
attack_steps: Exfil over C2: beacon sends data chunks in HTTP POST body or DNS TXT queries
Exfil via web service: upload to Mega/Dropbox/Google Drive using stolen API keys
Exfil via protocol tunneling: SSH tunnel DNS tunneling (iodine dnscat2)
Rate-limiting: exfiltrate slowly (low and slow) to avoid volume-based detection
Alternative: exfil via physical media (USB) or alternative protocols (ICMP NTP)

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect unusual outbound data volume new/unknown destinations DNS tunneling patterns and DLP policy violations
logs: Zeek conn.log — outbound connection volume analysis (bytes_out anomalies)
Zeek dns.log — DNS tunneling detection (high-entropy queries long domain names TXT record volume)
Zeek http.log / ssl.log — HTTPS connections to unknown/new destinations
DLP alerts — sensitive data patterns detected in outbound traffic
Sysmon Event 3 (Network Connection) — unexpected outbound connections
Firewall logs — egress traffic to non-standard destinations
detection_rules: Zeek/RITA: DNS tunneling detection (high entropy in subdomains unusual TXT record volume)
Sigma: net_connection_win_rclone_cloud — rclone.exe making connections to cloud storage
Splunk: index=zeek | stats sum(orig_bytes) by dest_ip | sort -sum(orig_bytes) — top data destinations
DLP: alert on credit card numbers SSNs classified keywords in outbound traffic

topics.gap_analysis: Encrypted exfiltration (HTTPS to legitimate cloud services) bypasses network-based DLP. DNS tunneling bypasses most network monitoring unless DNS-specific analysis is deployed. Slow exfiltration evades volume-based detection. Gap: many orgs allow broad egress access making it hard to identify anomalous destinations.
drills: Exfiltrate data via three methods: HTTPS POST to a C2 DNS tunneling with dnscat2 and cloud upload with rclone. For each identify which detection catches it. Implement DNS tunneling detection with Zeek/RITA. Set up egress filtering and show it blocks unexpected destinations.
common_mistakes: Not monitoring DNS for tunneling (only monitoring HTTP/HTTPS)
Allowing all egress HTTPS traffic (cant detect exfil to new destinations)
Not deploying DLP on endpoints (network-only DLP misses encrypted exfil)

topics.title: Screen Capture & Keylogging (T1113 T1056) vs. EDR Behavior Monitoring
concepts: Screen capture: taking screenshots of the user desktop to collect visual data (documents emails)
Keylogging: recording keystrokes to capture passwords messages and data entry
These techniques collect data without accessing files directly — harder to detect with file-based monitoring
EDR behavior monitoring: detects API calls associated with capture (BitBlt GetAsyncKeyState SetWindowsHookEx)
Windows API hooks used for capture can be detected via API call monitoring
key_facts: Screen capture uses GDI functions: BitBlt GetDC CreateCompatibleBitmap
Keylogging uses: SetWindowsHookEx (WH_KEYBOARD_LL) GetAsyncKeyState polling or kernel-mode filter drivers
Sysmon doesnt natively capture screen capture or keylogging API calls
EDR products monitor for suspicious API call patterns associated with these techniques

attack_side.technique: Capture screen content and keystrokes to collect sensitive data including credentials and communications
attack_steps: Screen capture: use PowerShell or C# to call BitBlt/GetDC and capture screen to image file
Keylogging: install keyboard hook via SetWindowsHookEx (WH_KEYBOARD_LL) or poll GetAsyncKeyState
Log captured data to file or exfiltrate via C2 channel
Periodic screen captures sent to C2 for analyst review

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect processes making screen capture API calls keyboard hook installation and clipboard access
logs: Sysmon Event 1 (Process Creation) — known capture tool execution
EDR API call monitoring — BitBlt GetAsyncKeyState SetWindowsHookEx OpenClipboard
Sysmon Event 11 (FileCreate) — image files (.png .jpg) created in unusual locations
Sysmon Event 7 (ImageLoaded) — gdi32.dll user32.dll loading by unusual processes
detection_rules: Sigma: proc_creation_win_screen_capture_tool — known screenshot tool execution from non-standard process
EDR: alert on SetWindowsHookEx from non-interactive/unusual processes
EDR: alert on BitBlt/GetDC calls from unexpected processes (not browsers not snipping tool)
Splunk: index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename=*.bmp OR *.png in temp directories
tools: EDR (API monitoring: CrowdStrike Defender for Endpoint)

topics.gap_analysis: Screen capture and keylogging use legitimate Windows APIs that also serve legitimate purposes creating false positives. Sysmon doesnt natively capture API calls — EDR is required for API-level detection. Gap: many EDRs dont alert on screen capture because too many legitimate apps take screenshots.
drills: Run a keylogger and screen capture tool in lab. Check which EDR alerts fire. If EDR doesnt catch it implement detection via Sysmon process monitoring and file creation analysis. Write rules for image file creation in temp by non-standard processes.
common_mistakes: Expecting Sysmon alone to detect keylogging (it cant — requires EDR API monitoring)
Not including clipboard monitoring (T1115) alongside keylogging
Ignoring audio/video capture (T1123 T1125) which are similar collection vectors

modules.title: C2 Infrastructure — Beaconing & DNS Tunneling vs. Network Traffic Analysis (Capstone)
modules.objective: Learner can establish C2 channels and detect them using Zeek network analysis, RITA beaconing detection, and DNS tunneling analytics, then run a complete purple team capstone exercise with BAS and metrics.

topics.title: C2 Beaconing (T1071.001) vs. RITA & Zeek Beaconing Detection
concepts: C2 beaconing: infected systems periodically contact a command and control server for instructions
Beacon patterns: regular intervals (jittered) specific data sizes consistent destinations
Common C2 protocols: HTTP/HTTPS (Cobalt Strike Empire) DNS (dnscat2) custom protocols
Zeek (Bro): network security monitor that logs all connection metadata (conn.log http.log ssl.log dns.log)
RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics): analyzes Zeek logs for beaconing DNS tunneling and long connections
key_facts: Beaconing detection: low-variance inter-arrival times and consistent data sizes are strong C2 indicators
Zeek conn.log captures every connection: timestamp duration source destination service bytes
RITA analyzes Zeek logs for statistical beaconing patterns (TS data size correlations)
Cobalt Strike default beacon profile: 60s sleep with 0-20% jitter — easily detectable by RITA

attack_side.technique: Establish a C2 channel via HTTP/HTTPS beaconing that mimics legitimate web traffic
attack_steps: Deploy C2 framework (Cobalt Strike Mythic Empire) with HTTPS listener
Configure beacon profile: user-agent sleep interval jitter (use high jitter to evade detection)
Execute beacon on victim: connects to C2 over HTTPS at regular intervals
C2 server issues commands; beacon executes and returns results in next check-in
Blend with legitimate traffic: use domain fronting or legitimate cloud services for C2 infrastructure

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect beaconing patterns: regular connection intervals consistent data sizes and connections to low-reputation domains
logs: Zeek conn.log — connection metadata for beaconing statistical analysis
Zeek ssl.log — TLS connections (JA3/JA3S fingerprinting for C2 identification)
Zeek http.log — HTTP request patterns and user-agent analysis
Firewall logs — periodic connections to same external destination
DNS logs — domain resolution patterns for C2 infrastructure
detection_rules: RITA: beaconing analysis from conn.log (low TS score indicates beaconing)
Zeek: JA3 fingerprint matching against known C2 frameworks (Cobalt Strike default JA3)
Splunk: index=zeek | stats avg(duration) stdev(duration) by id.orig_h id.resp_h | where stdev(duration) < threshold
Sigma: net_connection_win_c2_infrastructure — known C2 framework indicators
tools: MITRE D3FEND: Connection Timeout behavioral analysis

topics.gap_analysis: Domain fronting (using legitimate CDNs like Azure/AWS) makes C2 traffic look like it goes to trusted domains. TLS 1.3 and encrypted beacons hide payload content from TLS inspection. Gap: RITA beaconing detection requires Zeek deployment internally — many orgs only have Zeek at the perimeter missing internal C2. High-jitter beacons (50%+) evade statistical beaconing detection.
drills: Deploy Cobalt Strike with HTTPS beacon in lab. Configure different sleep/jitter settings (60s/0% 300s/20% 600s/50%). Run RITA analysis on Zeek logs. Which beacon profiles are detected? Write custom Zeek scripts for specific beacon patterns. Then use domain fronting and show how it evades destination-based detection.
common_mistakes: Not deploying Zeek internally (only at perimeter)
Only looking at destination IPs and not analyzing connection timing patterns
Forgetting JA3/JA3S fingerprinting which can identify C2 frameworks regardless of destination

topics.title: DNS Tunneling (T1071.004) vs. DNS Analytics & RITA
concepts: DNS tunneling: encoding data in DNS queries/responses to bypass firewall rules (DNS is almost always allowed outbound)
Data exfiltration via DNS: data encoded in subdomain labels of DNS queries (Base32/Hex encoding)
DNS C2: command data returned in TXT records or CNAME responses
Common tools: dnscat2 iodine DNScat Cobalt Strike DNS beacon
Detection: high-entropy subdomain labels unusual query volumes large TXT records and long domain names
key_facts: DNS queries have a 253-character limit but attackers split data across multiple queries
TXT records can carry up to 4096 bytes per response — enough for command data
iodine and dnscat2 are the most common DNS tunneling tools
RITA detects DNS tunneling by analyzing query lengths entropy and TXT record frequency from Zeek dns.log

attack_side.technique: Use DNS as a covert channel for C2 and data exfiltration encoding data in DNS queries and responses
attack_steps: Set up DNS tunneling server (iodine dnscat2) with authoritative DNS for a controlled domain
Execute client on victim: encodes data in subdomain queries (e.g., data1.data2.data3.evil.com)
Data exfiltration: file contents Base32-encoded and sent as DNS query labels
C2 commands: returned via TXT records from the authoritative server
Bypasses firewalls because DNS (port 53) is typically allowed outbound

defense_side.what_to_detect: Detect DNS tunneling via high-entropy subdomain labels unusual query volumes large TXT records and domains with excessive subdomain depth
logs: Zeek dns.log — DNS query metadata (query name type response)
Windows DNS Server debug/analytic logs
Firewall DNS logs
Sysmon Event 22 (DNS Query) — process-level DNS query attribution
detection_rules: RITA: DNS tunneling analysis (high entropy in subdomain labels long FQDNs excessive TXT records)
Zeek custom script: alert on DNS queries with subdomain entropy > threshold
Splunk: index=zeek | eval subdomain_len=len(query) | where subdomain_len > 50
Sigma: dns_query_win_long_domain — Sysmon Event 22 with unusually long domain names
DLP: monitor DNS traffic volume per host (hosts sending 100x normal DNS volume are suspicious)
controls: Firewall: restrict DNS to approved recursive resolvers only
Monitor DNS query entropy and volume
Response Policy Zones (RPZ) for DNS firewalling

topics.gap_analysis: DNS tunneling is hard to detect because DNS is essential and always allowed. Entropy-based detection catches obvious tunneling but sophisticated attackers use dictionary encoding (mapping data to dictionary words) to reduce entropy. Gap: many orgs dont collect Zeek DNS logs or analyze DNS query patterns at all. DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) further obscures DNS queries from network monitoring.
drills: Set up dnscat2 DNS tunnel in lab. Exfiltrate a file via DNS. Analyze Zeek dns.log — what patterns are visible? Run RITA and verify it detects the tunneling. Then try iodine with dictionary encoding — does entropy-based detection still work? Write custom detection rules.
common_mistakes: Not collecting or analyzing DNS logs at all
Allowing DNS to any resolver (not restricting to approved recursive resolvers)
Only looking at DNS query volume not entropy or query content patterns

topics.title: Breach & Attack Simulation (BAS) & Purple Team Metrics — MTTD, MTTR & Coverage
concepts: BAS (Breach and Attack Simulation): automated platforms that continuously run simulated attacks to validate security controls
Commercial BAS platforms: SafeBreach AttackIQ Cymulate Picus — automated ATT&CK-based simulation
Open-source BAS: Atomic Red Team CALDERA Prelude — manual or semi-automated simulation
MTTD (Mean Time to Detect): average time from attacker action to detection by the SOC
MTTR (Mean Time to Respond/Resolve): average time from detection to containment/remediation
Detection coverage percentage: percentage of relevant ATT&CK techniques with working detections
key_facts: SafeBreach simulates attacks across the kill chain and validates prevention/detection at each layer
AttackIQ was a founding partner of MITRE ATT&CK and has deep ATT&CK integration
Industry average MTTD is ~200 days; top-performing SOCs achieve <24 hours
Industry average MTTR is ~70 days; top-performing SOCs achieve <24 hours
Detection coverage should be measured per ATT&CK tactic: aim for >70% coverage on Initial Access Execution and Credential Access

attack_side.technique: Run continuous automated attack simulations to measure detection coverage gaps and validate existing controls
attack_steps: Configure BAS platform (e.g., SafeBreach) with ATT&CK technique library
Run simulation campaigns across all ATT&CK tactics
For each technique: record whether it was prevented detected or missed
Generate coverage heatmap showing gaps by ATT&CK tactic
Prioritize remediation: build new detections for the highest-risk gaps

defense_side.what_to_detect: Track detection coverage MTTD MTTR false positive rate and control effectiveness as ongoing KPIs
logs: All SIEM alerts correlated with BAS simulation timestamps
EDR detection logs
SOAR (Security Orchestration) response time tracking
detection_rules: BAS platform reporting: per-technique prevention/detection/miss results
SIEM metrics dashboard: MTTD = avg(time_alert - time_attack) across simulations
Coverage heatmap: percentage of ATT&CK techniques with at least one working detection
False positive rate: (false_alerts / total_alerts) per detection rule

topics.gap_analysis: BAS platforms test individual techniques but may not test full attack chains. MTTD/MTTR metrics can be gamed if detection/alerting thresholds are too loose (low MTTD but high false positives). Gap: many orgs measure detection coverage but dont measure response effectiveness (MTTR) or false positive impact on SOC analysts.
drills: Full capstone: Run a complete purple team exercise. Deploy CALDERA with an adversary profile (e.g., APT29 emulation). Execute the full attack chain. Measure: (1) detection coverage by tactic (2) MTTD per technique (3) MTTR for detected techniques. Generate a VECTR report and ATT&CK Navigator heatmap. Identify top 5 gaps and build new detections.
common_mistakes: Running BAS once and not continuously — controls degrade over time
Only measuring detection coverage and not MTTD/MTTR (speed matters as much as coverage)
Not tracking false positive rate alongside coverage (100% coverage with 90% false positives is useless)
Focusing on technique count rather than risk-prioritized coverage

topics.title: Tabletop Exercises & Cyber Range Scenarios — The Unicorn Capstone
concepts: Tabletop exercises: discussion-based scenarios where teams walk through incident response procedures without technical execution
Cyber range exercises: hands-on scenarios in isolated environments where red and blue teams execute in real-time
Hybrid exercises: combine tabletop discussion with live technical execution (purple team format)
CISA Tabletop Exercise Packages (CTEP): free customizable exercise templates with scenarios and injects
Scenario design: map exercise objectives to ATT&CK techniques and organizational risk
key_facts: CISA provides free tabletop exercise packages for ransomware phishing and supply chain scenarios
HTB (Hack The Box) Detection and OpSec Cyber Range provides purple team lab environments
Purple team exercises should be run quarterly minimum — continuous improvement cycle
Scenario realism: use threat intelligence to model exercises after real adversary behaviors

attack_side.technique: Execute a full adversary emulation scenario in a cyber range simulating a real threat actor campaign
attack_steps: Select threat actor to emulate (e.g., APT29 FIN7 LockBit)
Map adversary TTPs to ATT&CK techniques from threat intelligence reports
Build emulation plan: chain techniques from Initial Access through Exfiltration
Execute scenario in cyber range with red team running attacks and blue team detecting
Debrief: both sides discuss what worked what didnt and what to improve

defense_side.what_to_detect: Measure end-to-end detection coverage across the full attack chain and identify where the chain breaks
logs: All log sources active during the exercise (Sysmon Windows Security Zeek EDR SIEM)
SOAR playbook execution logs
Incident response timeline correlated with attack timestamps
detection_rules: Full detection suite tested against the emulation scenario
Correlation rules linking multiple techniques into attack chain alerts
controls: Full detection stack (SIEM + EDR + Sysmon + Zeek)

topics.gap_analysis: The capstone exercise reveals where detection coverage breaks across the kill chain. Common finding: detections exist for individual techniques but no correlation rule links them into an attack chain alert. Gap: many orgs detect individual techniques but miss the broader campaign narrative. Purple team exercises build these correlation detections.
drills: ULTIMATE CAPSTONE: Run a 2-day purple team exercise emulating a ransomware operator (e.g., LockBit). Day 1: Red team executes full attack chain (phishing to PowerShell to LSASS dump to PtH to data exfil to encryption). Blue team attempts detection and response in real-time. Track every technique in VECTR. Day 2: Joint debrief identifying gaps. Build new detections and correlation rules. Re-run the scenario to validate improvements. Final metrics: detection coverage MTTD MTTR and attack chain correlation.
common_mistakes: Running exercises without clear objectives or success criteria
Not involving both teams in the debrief and improvement process
Failing to follow up on identified gaps with actual detection improvements
Using unrealistic scenarios that dont match organizational threat landscape
